lead: No natural product has grade A evidence in osteoarthritis. Glucosamine and chondroitin have been tested in large trials: industry-independent and large trials found little or no benefit over placebo for knee or hip pain, while smaller and commercially funded trials were more positive (grade B, mixed results). A 2026 Cochrane review found that turmeric may make little to no difference to knee pain. Boswellia reduced pain compared with placebo in a Cochrane analysis of two small trials (85 people), pooled collagen trials found better pain scores than with placebo but with results that varied a lot between trials, and avocado-soybean unsaponifiables produced a small and clinically questionable improvement in symptoms (all four grade B).

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo

disclaimer: This page summarizes published research. It is not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

products.name: Avocado-soybean unsaponifiables (ASU)
products.summary: A 2014 Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence from four trials (651 people) that ASU 300 mg produced a small and clinically questionable improvement in symptoms after three to 12 months, with no difference from placebo in joint space width in two trials. A 2008 meta-analysis of four trials, all supported by the manufacturer, in 664 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis found less pain with ASU, with heterogeneous results and better chances of success in knee than in hip osteoarthritis. A 2019 meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials likewise found a benefit in knee but not in hip osteoarthritis.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review found probably no increase in adverse events compared with placebo, and the 2019 meta-analysis found similar adverse events with ASU and placebo. A 2019 safety meta-analysis noted that all eligible ASU studies allowed other osteoarthritis medicines, so that the safety of ASU still needs confirming in studies without them. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Avocado-soybean unsaponifiables
general_safety.short: In a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled osteoarthritis trials, adverse events were no more common than with placebo. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Boswellia
products.summary: A 2014 Cochrane review found high-quality evidence from two small trials (85 people) that 90 days of an enriched Boswellia serrata extract (100 mg) reduced pain by 17 points on a 100-point scale compared with placebo. A 2020 meta-analysis of 7 trials in 545 people found that boswellia may relieve pain compared with control groups. A 2024 meta-analysis of 13 knee trials found no significant overall effect, which the authors attributed to high heterogeneity, but a benefit over placebo in subgroup analysis. A 2018 meta-analysis found boswellia more effective than placebo but rated study quality low. A 2025 network meta-analysis of knee trials ranked boswellia as having the highest probability of being most effective for pain and stiffness among seven supplements and called for larger trials.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review reported no serious adverse events but was uncertain whether adverse events or withdrawals were more common with boswellia because reporting varied between studies. The 2018 meta-analysis found no significant differences from placebo in safety outcomes. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Boswellia
general_safety.short: In meta-analyses of knee osteoarthritis trials, adverse events did not differ from placebo. A review lists it among herbs with case reports of severe adverse effects when taken with warfarin.

products.name: Chondroitin
products.summary: A 2015 Cochrane review of 43 randomized trials, most in knee osteoarthritis and most of low quality, found that chondroitin was better than placebo for pain in short-term studies. The benefit became uncertain when the analysis was limited to trials with a large sample, appropriate allocation concealment or no pharmaceutical funding. A 2007 meta-analysis of 20 trials (3,846 people, knee or hip) found that small and less rigorous trials showed larger effects; in the 3 large trials analyzed by intention to treat, the effect was close to zero. In a 24-week five-arm trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis, chondroitin sulfate (1200 mg daily) was not significantly better than placebo. In a 6-month randomized trial in 162 people with hand osteoarthritis, chondroitin sulfate (800 mg daily) reduced hand pain and improved hand function more than placebo.
products.safety_interactions: The 2015 Cochrane review found a lower risk of serious adverse events with chondroitin than with control, and the 2007 meta-analysis found no difference from placebo in the risk of any adverse event. In the hand osteoarthritis trial, safety end points did not differ between groups. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies of chondroitin alone.

general_safety.name: Chondroitin
general_safety.short: In a review of 43 trials, adverse events were no more common than with placebo. With glucosamine, it is linked to bleeding risk and raised INR in people on anticoagulants such as warfarin.

products.name: Collagen (undenatured type II collagen and collagen peptides)
products.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials in 870 people with knee osteoarthritis found better function and pain scores with oral collagen than with placebo, with results that varied a lot between trials. A 2019 meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials found lower total WOMAC and pain visual analog scores with collagen, but no significant difference in the WOMAC pain or functional limitation subscores. In a 180-day randomized, double-blind trial in 191 people with knee osteoarthritis, an undenatured type II collagen supplement lowered the overall WOMAC score more than placebo. A 2018 meta-analysis of supplements found that undenatured type II collagen was one of only two with clinically important effects on pain at medium term, and that no supplement had clinically important effects on pain at long term.
products.safety_interactions: In the 191-person trial, safety outcomes did not differ among the groups. The 2018 meta-analysis found no differences between supplements and placebo for safety outcomes, apart from one non-collagen product. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Collagen
general_safety.short: In osteoarthritis trials the most reported adverse events were mild to moderate gastrointestinal complaints; a review of 11 skin trials reported no adverse events.

products.name: Curcumin (turmeric)
products.summary: A 2026 Cochrane review included 9 randomized trials in 1,245 people, all with knee osteoarthritis and none longer than three months. In the four placebo-controlled trials, turmeric may result in little to no difference in pain, function or quality of life (low-certainty evidence): pain was 0.72 points lower on a 0 to 10 scale, short of the 1.5 points taken as clinically significant. Turmeric may improve participant-reported treatment success, based on low-certainty evidence from 2 trials in 170 people. Earlier meta-analyses were more positive: a 2021 meta-analysis of 15 trials in 1,621 people found lower pain and better function than with placebo and effects similar to anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), and a 2018 meta-analysis found benefit over placebo but rated study quality low, with most trials enrolling fewer than 100 people. No trials in hand or hip osteoarthritis were included in the Cochrane review.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review was very uncertain about the effect of turmeric on adverse events, withdrawals and serious adverse events. The 2021 meta-analysis found adverse events comparable with placebo and reported that adding curcumin to NSAIDs did not increase adverse events compared with NSAIDs alone. The 2018 meta-analysis found fewer gastrointestinal adverse events with curcuminoids than with NSAIDs. Interactions with other medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Turmeric and curcumin
general_safety.short: Case series link turmeric supplements to liver injury, sometimes severe. Curcumin may alter levels of some drugs, including anticoagulants, mostly in non-clinical studies.

products.name: Ginger
products.summary: A 2015 meta-analysis of five randomized placebo-controlled trials in 593 people found a statistically significant reduction in pain and disability with oral ginger, described by the authors as modestly efficacious, and rated the evidence moderate quality. A 2020 meta-analysis in knee osteoarthritis found less pain with ginger capsules than with placebo but no significant difference in knee function, and concluded there was insufficient evidence to support oral ginger. A 2022 meta-analysis of three trials found that pain was the only clinical measure that fell significantly.
products.safety_interactions: In the 2015 meta-analysis, people given ginger were more than twice as likely to stop treatment as those given placebo; the authors still described ginger as reasonably safe. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Ginger
general_safety.short: Pregnancy trials found no significant rise in miscarriage (with wide uncertainty), heartburn or drowsiness. A warfarin review flags possible added bleeding risk.

products.name: Glucosamine
products.summary: Results are mixed and depend on trial size and funding. A 2017 meta-analysis of individual patient data from five industry-independent trials (1,625 people) found glucosamine no better than placebo for knee or hip pain or function at 3 months or 24 months. A 2010 network meta-analysis of 10 large trials in 3,803 people with knee or hip osteoarthritis found a pain difference of 0.4 cm on a 10 cm scale, smaller than the 0.9 cm set in advance as clinically important, with smaller effects in industry-independent trials. In a 24-week five-arm trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis, glucosamine (1500 mg daily) was not significantly better than placebo. A 2005 Cochrane review of 20 trials found a pooled improvement in pain, but not in the eight trials with adequate allocation concealment. A 2018 network meta-analysis of knee trials lasting at least 12 months found an association between glucosamine sulfate and less pain, with large uncertainty.
products.safety_interactions: The 2005 Cochrane review found glucosamine as safe as placebo in the number of people reporting adverse reactions, and a 2019 safety meta-analysis concluded that glucosamine sulfate can be considered safe for people with osteoarthritis. A 2008 case report and review of adverse-event databases found reports of raised INR (a measure of blood clotting time) in people taking warfarin together with glucosamine or glucosamine plus chondroitin, and concluded that the combination of warfarin and glucosamine may raise INR.

general_safety.name: Glucosamine
general_safety.short: As safe as placebo for adverse reactions in a review of 20 trials. Reports suggest it may raise INR in people on warfarin; evidence on blood glucose effects is mixed.

products.name: Glucosamine plus chondroitin
products.summary: In a 24-week randomized trial of 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis that compared glucosamine, chondroitin, both together, celecoxib and placebo, the combination was not significantly better than placebo overall; an exploratory analysis found a higher response rate in the subgroup with moderate-to-severe pain. A 2010 network meta-analysis of large knee and hip trials found a pain difference of 0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale for the combination and concluded that it does not reduce joint pain. A 2023 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials in 3,793 people with knee osteoarthritis found a better total WOMAC score with the combination than with placebo but no significant difference in pain on a visual analog scale. A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled 3 trials of the combination found no reduction in pain and no improvement in function.
products.safety_interactions: In the 1,583-person trial, adverse events were mild, infrequent and evenly spread across groups, and the 2023 meta-analysis found no significant safety differences. A 2008 case report and review of adverse-event databases described raised INR and bleeding or bruising in people taking warfarin together with glucosamine or glucosamine plus chondroitin.

general_safety.name: Glucosamine
general_safety.short: As safe as placebo for adverse reactions in a review of 20 trials. Reports suggest it may raise INR in people on warfarin; evidence on blood glucose effects is mixed.

general_safety.name: Chondroitin
general_safety.short: In a review of 43 trials, adverse events were no more common than with placebo. With glucosamine, it is linked to bleeding risk and raised INR in people on anticoagulants such as warfarin.

products.name: Green-lipped mussel extract
products.summary: A 2021 systematic review included nine clinical trials of green-lipped mussel extract in osteoarthritis and pooled five of them: pain on a visual analogue scale was lower with the extract (effect size -0.46), which the authors called a moderate and clinically meaningful effect, while noting that the evidence is limited by the number and quality of studies. An earlier systematic review of four randomized trials set aside two because of possible un-blinding and inappropriate statistical analysis, and concluded from the two more rigorous trials that the extract may be superior to placebo in mild to moderate osteoarthritis. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 100 adults with knee osteoarthritis, green-lipped mussel powder (1,000 mg a day) improved pain and physical function more than placebo; the primary outcome, total WOMAC score, was significantly better only in the analysis limited to the 93 people who completed the study.
products.safety_interactions: The 2021 systematic review reported that the extract was considered generally well tolerated in most studies, and the 100-person trial identified no clinically meaningful safety concerns. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Green-lipped mussel extract
general_safety.short: Generally well tolerated in most of nine osteoarthritis trials. A case report describes an allergic reaction after inhaling the powder; the mussel contains potentially allergenic proteins.

products.name: L-carnitine
products.summary: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in 619 people with osteoarthritis found better WOMAC function, total WOMAC and pain scores with L-carnitine than in control groups; the authors rated the quality of the included studies as mediocre and found heterogeneity between them. In a 12-week double-blind randomized trial in 76 obese women with knee osteoarthritis who were all on a low-calorie diet, L-carnitine (1000 mg) did not differ from placebo in pain, stiffness, physical function or total scores.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine
general_safety.short: In neuropathy trials, adverse events with acetyl-L-carnitine were similar to placebo; L-carnitine taken for 12 to 24 weeks raised blood TMAO, a compound linked to atherosclerosis.

products.name: MSM (methylsulfonylmethane)
products.summary: The trials of MSM alone are small. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind pilot trial in 50 people with knee osteoarthritis pain, MSM (3 g twice a day) lowered WOMAC pain and physical function impairment more than placebo, with no notable change in stiffness. In another 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 49 people with knee osteoarthritis (1.125 g three times daily), physical function and total WOMAC scores improved more with MSM, WOMAC pain did not differ significantly, and the authors called the improvements small and of undetermined clinical significance. A 2008 systematic review described the evidence as positive but not definitive, and a 2018 meta-analysis of supplements placed MSM among those with statistically significant pain improvements of unclear clinical importance. In a 12-week randomized trial in 106 people with hand osteoarthritis, a combination of boswellia, pine bark extract, MSM and curcumin did not reduce hand pain more than placebo. Graded B because two randomized, double-blind trials each found some benefit over placebo; both were small, one was a pilot, their results for pain differed and the clinical importance of the improvements is undetermined.
products.safety_interactions: The 50-person pilot trial reported no major adverse events and stated that the safety of long-term use could not be confirmed. In the hand osteoarthritis trial of the four-ingredient combination, 10% of the supplement group and 7% of the placebo group stopped treatment because of adverse events. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)
general_safety.short: A review describes few known and mild side effects; a 16-week placebo-controlled trial found no changes in blood, liver or kidney tests. Long-term safety is unconfirmed.

products.name: Omega-3 (fish oil and krill oil)
products.summary: A 2023 meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials in 2,070 people with osteoarthritis found less pain and better joint function with omega-3 supplements than with placebo, while a 2022 meta-analysis of nutritional supplements reported that omega-3 caused no changes in osteoarthritis measures. For krill oil in knee osteoarthritis, a 24-week randomized trial in 262 people with significant knee pain and effusion-synovitis found that 2 g a day did not improve knee pain compared with placebo, whereas a 6-month trial in 235 adults with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis found modest improvements in pain, stiffness and function with 4 g a day. A 2025 meta-analysis of 5 krill oil trials (730 people) found no significant improvement on a pain visual analog scale but better WOMAC pain, stiffness and function scores than with usual care. A two-year trial in 202 people compared high-dose with low-dose fish oil, without a placebo group, and found no additional benefit of the high dose.
products.safety_interactions: The 2023 meta-analysis reported no severe treatment-related adverse events and a similar rate of adverse events in both groups. In the 262-person krill oil trial, adverse events were reported by 51% of the krill oil group and 54% of the placebo group. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Omega-3 fatty acids
general_safety.short: Linked to a higher risk of atrial fibrillation in cardiovascular trials, more so above 1 g/day; diarrhoea and altered taste were more likely than with placebo; bleeding findings are mixed.

products.name: Probiotics
products.summary: Results differ by strain and the trials are few. A 2024 meta-analysis of three randomized studies (501 people) found fewer symptoms with one Lactobacillus casei strain but no apparent effect with the other probiotics reviewed. A 2025 meta-analysis of five randomized trials in 694 people with knee osteoarthritis found lower total WOMAC and pain scores than in control groups, with no significant difference in stiffness, and said the results need validating in large studies. In a 12-week randomized, triple-blind trial in 70 overweight or obese people with knee osteoarthritis, Saccharomyces boulardii reduced pain more than placebo, and in a 12-week exploratory randomized, double-blind trial in 100 people with chronic knee pain, a Latilactobacillus sakei strain improved WOMAC and pain scores more than placebo.
products.safety_interactions: A 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis found no significant difference in adverse events between probiotics and placebo and no serious safety issues. The Saccharomyces boulardii trial reported no severe side effects and the Latilactobacillus sakei trial observed no adverse events. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Probiotics
general_safety.short: Trials have not shown increased risk, though safety reporting is weak. Rare bloodstream infections occur, mainly in people who are severely ill, immunosuppressed or in intensive care.

products.name: Resveratrol
products.summary: In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at three centers, 142 adults with painful knee osteoarthritis took oral resveratrol (40 mg twice a day for a week, then 20 mg twice a day) or placebo. At 3 months the reduction in knee pain was almost identical in the two groups; the authors noted that the trial was underpowered. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial in 110 people with knee osteoarthritis, resveratrol (500 mg a day) added to the anti-inflammatory drug meloxicam improved pain and function more than placebo added to meloxicam over 90 days. A 16-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 123 people aged 63 to 75 reported lower WOMAC scores and less pain during walking with resveratrol (500 mg a day); its abstract does not state how these changes compared with the placebo group.
products.safety_interactions: In the 142-person trial, serious adverse events, judged unrelated to the interventions, occurred in 3 people in the resveratrol group and 2 in the placebo group. The trial of resveratrol added to meloxicam reported that the combination was safe and well tolerated on clinical and biochemical markers. Interactions with medicines were not otherwise reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Resveratrol
general_safety.short: Generally well tolerated up to 1 g/day; 2.5 to 5 g/day caused mild to moderate gut symptoms. Changes CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP1A2 activity, so may interact with medicines.

products.name: Rose hip powder
products.summary: A 2008 meta-analysis pooled three randomized trials of rose hip powder in 287 people, all supported by the manufacturer, with a median duration of 3 months. Pain scores fell more with rose hip powder than with placebo, with consistent results across the trials; the authors called the data sparse and asked for independent replication in a large, long-term trial. In a randomized, double-blind crossover trial in 94 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis, 5 g of rose hip powder daily reduced WOMAC pain compared with placebo after 3 weeks.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Rose hip
general_safety.short: A mechanism-focused review states that trials showed excellent tolerability; a meta-analysis of three manufacturer-supported trials said safety still needs a large, long-term trial.

products.name: SAMe (S-adenosylmethionine)
products.summary: A 2009 Cochrane review of four placebo-controlled trials in 656 people with knee or hip osteoarthritis found a small difference in pain that was not statistically significant and no clear effect on function. The reviewers judged the trials to be of poor quality, called the review inconclusive and advised against routine use. A 2002 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials found that SAMe improved functional limitation, but not pain, compared with placebo, based on only 2 studies, and that it appeared comparable with NSAIDs.
products.safety_interactions: In the Cochrane review, the numbers of people with adverse events or withdrawing because of them did not differ significantly from placebo, with wide confidence intervals, and no trial reported on serious adverse events. In the 2002 meta-analysis, people taking SAMe were less likely to report adverse effects than those taking NSAIDs. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe)
general_safety.short: Dropout rates in depression trials were similar to placebo or antidepressants. A review says it is contraindicated in bipolar disorder; a case report describes mania with an SSRI.

citations.label: Rutjes et al., 2009, Cochrane Database Syst Rev
citations.title: S-Adenosylmethionine for osteoarthritis of the knee or hip.

citations.label: Soeken et al., 2002, J Fam Pract
citations.title: Safety and efficacy of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) for osteoarthritis.

products.name: Vitamin C
products.summary: In a multicenter, double-blind, randomized crossover trial, 133 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis took one gram of calcium ascorbate or placebo daily for about 14 days each. Pain was 4.6 mm lower on a 100 mm scale with calcium ascorbate than with placebo, an effect the authors described as less than half that commonly reported for NSAIDs. In a prospective cohort study, self-reported vitamin C supplement use was not associated with progression of existing knee osteoarthritis, although users without knee osteoarthritis at the start were less likely to develop it. A 2021 review called the data controversial and said more randomized placebo-controlled trials are needed. Graded B because the multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial found a statistically significant benefit; each treatment period lasted only about 14 days, so the trial does not show whether the effect lasts with longer use.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Vitamin C
general_safety.short: Cohort data link supplemental vitamin C to a higher risk of kidney stones in men but not in women. A review advises caution with high doses in susceptible people.

citations.label: Jensen et al., 2003, Ugeskr Laeger

citations.title: The effects of vitamin C supplementation on incident and progressive knee osteoarthritis: a longitudinal study.

products.name: Vitamin D
products.summary: A 2017 meta-analysis of four randomized trials (570 people given vitamin D and 560 given placebo), all rated at low risk of bias, found a statistically significant but small-to-moderate effect on knee pain and concluded that vitamin D may not have a clinically significant effect on pain or on structural progression. A 2021 meta-analysis of six reports covering 1,599 people with knee osteoarthritis found better WOMAC pain and function scores with vitamin D but no significant change in cartilage volume or joint space width. The trials were in knee osteoarthritis.
products.safety_interactions: A second 2017 meta-analysis of four randomized trials (1,136 people) found no significant difference in the incidence of adverse events between the vitamin D and placebo groups. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Vitamin D
general_safety.short: Long-term supplementation raised the risk of high blood calcium and high urine calcium in trials, but not kidney stones; toxicity from extremely high doses is rare but serious.

products.name: Ashwagandha
products.summary: One small randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was found. Sixty people with knee joint pain and discomfort (the abstract does not say that osteoarthritis was confirmed) took one of two doses of an ashwagandha root and leaf extract or placebo for 12 weeks; knee symptom and swelling scores fell compared with baseline and placebo at both doses. A 2025 network meta-analysis of botanical extracts for knee osteoarthritis reported that ashwagandha extract reduced stiffness scores compared with placebo. Graded C because the evidence rests on a single small trial.
products.safety_interactions: The 60-person trial reported that all treatments were well tolerated. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Ashwagandha
general_safety.short: Case reports link ashwagandha to liver injury (jaundice, itching), with deaths in people who already had cirrhosis, and to thyrotoxicosis in one reported case.

citations.title: A randomized, double blind placebo controlled study of efficacy and tolerability of Withaina somnifera extracts in knee joint pain.

citations.label: Yan et al., 2025, Front Pharmacol
citations.title: Efficacy of botanical extracts for knee osteoarthritis: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

products.name: Creatine
products.summary: Creatine has been tested in small trials, two of them alongside exercise. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis who all followed a lower limb resistance training program, physical function improved more with creatine than with placebo, while pain fell in both groups. In a four-week double-blind randomized trial in 40 people with knee osteoarthritis receiving physical therapy and resistance exercise, pain and overall knee scores favored the creatine group. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 18 people with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis, creatine did not differ from placebo in knee symptom scores or muscle strength. Graded C because the trials are small and the positive ones tested creatine together with exercise.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Creatine
general_safety.short: Creatine is associated with a small rise in blood creatinine, described as transient, without a significant change in kidney filtration; no serious adverse outcomes in studies of women.

citations.label: Cornish et al., 2018, Nutr Res
citations.title: No effect of creatine monohydrate supplementation on inflammatory and cartilage degradation biomarkers in individuals with knee osteoarthritis.

products.name: Pine bark extract
products.summary: A 2020 Cochrane review of pine bark extract found three osteoarthritis trials with 293 people and rated the evidence for knee osteoarthritis very low certainty, concluding that no definitive conclusions about efficacy or safety are possible. In one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 100 people with knee osteoarthritis took 150 mg of pine bark extract a day or placebo for 3 months; the abstract reports within-group improvement in WOMAC and pain scores with the extract and no effect of placebo, without a direct comparison between the groups. In a 12-week randomized trial in 106 people with hand osteoarthritis, a combination of boswellia, pine bark extract, MSM and curcumin did not reduce hand pain more than placebo. Graded C because the only supportive result in a cited abstract is a within-group change and the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low certainty.
products.safety_interactions: The 100-person trial described the extract as well tolerated. The Cochrane review concluded that no definitive conclusions about the safety of pine bark extract are possible. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Pine bark extract
general_safety.short: A systematic review of 15 small trials (791 participants) could draw no definitive conclusions about safety. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Bromelain
products.summary: The one placebo-controlled trial found was a small pilot. In it, 47 people with moderate to severe knee osteoarthritis were randomized to 12 weeks of bromelain (800 mg a day) or placebo in addition to their usual treatment, and 31 completed the trial. There were no statistically significant differences between groups in the total WOMAC score, its subscales or quality of life, and the authors noted that the study's limitations support the need for a follow-up study. In a randomized, single-blind pilot study in 40 people with knee osteoarthritis that compared bromelain (500 mg a day) with diclofenac and had no placebo group, WOMAC scores did not differ between the groups after 4 weeks and the authors called the treatment difference inconclusive; the improvement reported at week 16 is a within-group change from baseline.
products.safety_interactions: In the placebo-controlled pilot trial, adverse events were generally mild in nature. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Bromelain
general_safety.short: Reported adverse events with oral use were flatulence, nausea and headache. A warfarin review lists it among products that may raise bleeding risk, based mostly on lab, animal or single-case data.

citations.label: Kasemsuk et al., 2016, Clin Rheumatol
citations.title: Improved WOMAC score following 16-week treatment with bromelain for knee osteoarthritis.

products.name: Vitamin E
products.summary: In a six-month double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 77 people with knee osteoarthritis, vitamin E (500 IU a day) showed no benefit over placebo for pain, stiffness or function at one, three or six months. In a 2-year double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 136 people with knee osteoarthritis, vitamin E (500 IU) did not change the loss of tibial cartilage volume, and symptom improvement did not differ from placebo. A 2022 meta-analysis of nutritional supplements reported that vitamin E caused no changes in osteoarthritis measures.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Vitamin E
general_safety.short: Meta-analyses link vitamin E to more haemorrhagic strokes and, at high doses, higher mortality; in the SELECT trial it raised prostate cancer risk in healthy men.
